feedback: If a learner predicted an instant catch and is surprised by the missed centimetres, connect the gap to the pathway: the delay is the time for detection, brain processing, and the response signal to the hand.
Link the felt reaction (jumping at a bang, catching a dropped object) back to the three-stage model so the abstract pathway maps onto a real reaction.
Treat the centimetres missed as a rough, qualitative sign of the delay — it varies by person and setup and is not a precise neural measurement.
activities.intendedInsight: There is a processing delay: the signal must travel from the eye to the brain, be processed, and travel back to the muscles — you cannot respond instantly, which shows the brain sits between sensing and responding.
learnerActions: One child holds a ruler vertically; the partner's fingers wait open at the zero mark ready to catch it when it is released without warning.
Before trying, PREDICT whether you can catch it the instant it is released, and explain why or why not.
Run several catches, note roughly how many centimetres slip past before you catch it, and discuss what the gap shows.
activities.title: Feel your own reaction-time loop (dropped-ruler test)

feedback: A strong answer: the ears detect the sound, but the brain processes and interprets it and decides the response; because each animal's brain handles the information differently, the same stimulus can lead to different responses.

Watch for the common wrong answer that 'the sense organ decides the response' — it is the brain, not the ear, that decides. If a learner skips processing (ears make the legs move with no brain), re-insert the brain between the sense organ and the response.
If a learner says the two animals must do the same thing because they heard the same sound, redirect to the processing step: the response depends on how the brain interprets the information.
activities.intendedInsight: A full explanation identifies the brain-processing step as the reason the same input can produce different outputs, and applies the pathway to a new animal or sense.
learnerActions: Put the stages of the pathway in order: stimulus → sense organ (receptor) → brain → response.
Match each animal to its special sense (bat→echolocation, dog→smell, migrating bird→magnetic sense, snake/spider→vibration).

Answer: a rabbit and a deer both hear the exact same twig snap; the rabbit freezes and the deer bolts. They received the same sound — so why did they do different things, and what must happen between the ears hearing the snap and the body moving?
Draw the journey of the twig-snap information from the forest to the animal responding, labelling each stage.
activities.title: Explain and consolidate: order the pathway and answer the discriminating case
